vignette:
Alex presents as a man who has built his life around the principle of running toward a fire, not away from it. At the station, he is known for his steadiness, a reassuring presence in the controlled chaos of an emergency call. This reputation for competence is what led him to volunteer two years ago with an international relief organization. He had his paramedic certification, extensive experience with trauma and extraction, and a deeply ingrained need to be useful. He was deployed for six weeks to a city shattered by conflict, a landscape of skeletal buildings and streets choked with debris.

He doesn't talk about the deployment as a whole, but rather in fractured, sensory snapshots. He speaks of the dust, a constant presence that coated his tongue and turned the air a hazy, perpetual gray. It was, he says, the dust of people’s lives—their homes, their possessions, their history, all pulverized. His training had prepared him for structural collapses and contained fires, for protocols and clear objectives. It had not prepared him for the sheer scale of the suffering, or for the agonizing choices of who to help when everyone needed helping.

The memory that surfaces most often, the one that ambushes him in the quiet of the firehouse bunk room at 3 a.m., is not of a dramatic rescue, but of a failure. He was helping clear the rubble of a collapsed apartment block when he found a little girl, no older than six, pinned by a concrete beam. She was conscious, her wide, dark eyes fixed on him. She was wearing a small blue coat. For two hours, he and his team worked, talking to her, promising her she’d be okay. He remembers the feel of the rebar he was trying to cut, the vibration buzzing up his arms. He remembers the dust motes dancing in the beam of his headlamp. And then, a tremor from a nearby blast shifted the rubble. The space they had painstakingly created vanished. He never saw her eyes again.

When he returned home, his wife, Sarah, threw a small party. He remembers standing in his own living room, a beer growing warm in his hand, listening to friends complain about property taxes and a canceled flight. The disconnect was so profound it felt like a physical pressure in his chest. He felt an intense, burning rage at their triviality, followed immediately by a wave of shame for feeling it. He excused himself and spent the rest of the evening in the garage, meticulously cleaning tools that were already clean.

Now, two years later, Alex moves through his life like a ghost. At work, he is hyper-focused, his vigilance honed to a razor's edge. He checks equipment three, four times. On a call, he is flawless, but afterward, the adrenaline doesn't subside. It curdles into a low-grade hum of anxiety that never quite shuts off. The scent of diesel exhaust or the sight of concrete dust at a construction site can drop him right back into that ruined city, the taste of chalk on his tongue.

At home, he is distant. Sarah tries to reach him, but he feels separated from her by a thick pane of glass. When she touches him, he flinches almost imperceptibly. He knows it hurts her, and that knowledge adds another layer to the immense guilt he carries—guilt for the girl in the blue coat, guilt for the ones he couldn't save, and guilt for being a shadow of the husband he once was. He avoids crowded places, and a car backfiring down the street sends him diving for cover in his own mind. Sleep offers little escape, often bringing nightmares of shifting rubble and a small blue coat. He spends most nights on the couch, watching infomercials until dawn, because he has learned that exhaustion is the only thing that can quiet the noise in his head.
